title: Matter, Spectra & the Doppler Effect
intro: Light carries clues about the matter that made it. Here you learn what atoms are made of, how matter changes phase, how electrons jump between energy levels, what the three kinds of spectra look like, and how the Doppler effect turns a tiny shift in a spectral line into a speed.

sections.title: Inside an atom

img.alt: A fuzzy dark ball for a helium atom with a zoom box showing four tiny particles at its centre.

steps.title: A helium atom up close
bullets: An atom has a tiny **nucleus** in the middle, made of **protons** (positive charge) and **neutrons** (no charge).
The nucleus is surrounded by an **electron cloud**. Electrons carry negative charge.
The nucleus is far smaller than the whole atom, so an atom is mostly empty space. The scale bar shows 1 angstrom = 100 picometres.

boxes.text: Why a cloud and not tiny planets on tracks? You cannot pin down exactly where an electron is, so its position is smeared out into a cloud. That cloud gives the atom its size, even though the electrons hold only a tiny part of its mass.
Positive protons and Neutral neutrons sit in the middle. The negative electrons stay outside, around them.

Do not draw electrons as planets orbiting the nucleus. Slide 2 and the textbook both use the electron-cloud picture. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. The slide writes the charge as +e and -e.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 5.3 (structure of matter, pp. 145-146; Fig 5.9)
The slide scale bar says 1 A = 100 pm; the zoom box (1 fm) shows the nucleus.

images.alt: A fuzzy dark ball for a helium atom with a zoom box showing four tiny particles at its centre.

sections.title: Atomic number, isotopes and ions

img.alt: Hydrogen, helium and carbon atoms, each with an electron cloud and a nucleus, labelled with atomic number, atomic mass number and electron count.

steps.title: Counting protons and neutrons
bullets: **Atomic number** = number of protons. It tells you which element the atom is: hydrogen 1, helium 2, carbon 6.
**Atomic mass number** = protons + neutrons. Helium-4 is 2 + 2 = 4 and carbon-12 is 6 + 6 = 12.
A **molecule** is two or more atoms chemically bonded together, such as H2O or CO2.

img.alt: Three carbon nuclei, carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14, each with 6 protons and 6, 7 or 8 neutrons.

steps.title: Isotopes and ions
bullets: **Isotopes** have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 all have 6 protons, with 6, 7 and 8 neutrons.
An **ion** has the same number of protons but a different number of electrons, such as He2+ or Cl-.
Charge = protons minus electrons. Losing electrons leaves an ion positive.

boxes.text: Why is the proton count the atom's name tag? Every atom of an element has exactly the same number of protons, while the neutron count can vary. So carbon-12 and carbon-14 are still both carbon, just with different weights.
Protons name the element. Neutrons change the weight (isotope). Electrons change the charge (ion).

Do not mix up atomic number (protons only) with atomic mass number (protons + neutrons). Wrong options on the practice test reuse the neutron count as the mass number or swap the two numbers. 'Doubly ionized' means 2 electrons LOST, so the charge is 2+, not 2-.

sourceNotes: Practice test 2 Q18 (Ca-44), practice questions Q25 (carbon-12 and carbon-14)

img.alt: Water molecules leaving an ocean surface into the air, while other molecules from the air drop back in.

steps.title: Phase depends on heat and pressure
bullets: The phase of a substance (solid, liquid or gas) depends on both **temperature** and **pressure**.
In the picture, water molecules keep leaving the ocean while others from the air drop back in.
Squeezing a gas at the same temperature can push its molecules close enough to turn it into a liquid.

img.alt: Photos of ice cubes, liquid water, a steaming pot, lightning and a Bose-Einstein condensate graph.

steps.title: Familiar, less familiar and exotic
bullets: **Familiar** phases: solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (steam).
**Less familiar**: **plasma**, found in lightning and stars.
**Exotic**: **Bose-Einstein condensates**, reached only near 0 Kelvin.

boxes.text: Why does heating change the phase? Heat raises the average energy of motion of the particles, so more of them can break free of the bonds that hold them to their neighbours.
Think of a crowd. Cold: everyone locked arm in arm (solid). Warmer: holding hands loosely (liquid). Hot: everyone running around free (gas).

Pressure alone does not make a plasma or ionize a gas. That needs very high temperature. Practice test 2 Q19: squeezing a gas at constant temperature could make it a liquid. Textbook extras: some evaporation always happens below the boiling point, and plasma can also be called a gas (the Sun is 'hot gas' or 'plasma'). Slide 6 only names the phases; the temperature link comes from slide 7.

images.alt: Water molecules leaving an ocean surface into the air, while other molecules from the air drop back in.
Photos of ice cubes, liquid water, a steaming pot, lightning and a Bose-Einstein condensate graph.

sections.title: Phase changes as things heat up
sections.slides: Matter deck (Ch5.3_PropertiesOfMatter.pdf) slide 7; Cosmic Perspective 5.3 p.148 Fig 5.10

img.alt: A tall red arrow labelled increasing temperature, with pictures of the solid, liquid, gas, molecular dissociation, plasma and fully ionized plasma stages stacked from bottom to top.

steps.title: From solid to plasma
bullets: Going up the temperature arrow: **melting** breaks rigid bonds (solid to liquid) and **evaporation** breaks flexible bonds (liquid to gas).
Hotter still: **dissociation** breaks molecules into atoms.
Hotter again: **ionization** strips electrons off atoms and leaves a **plasma** made of ions.

steps.title: Ionizing more than once
bullets: A neutral atom can lose more than one electron. Hydrogen has only one electron, so it can be ionized only once and is left as a bare proton, H+.
Oxygen has 8 protons. **Singly ionized** oxygen, O+, has lost 1 electron (7 left, charge +1). **Doubly ionized** oxygen, O2+, has lost 2 (6 left, charge +2).
At millions of K every electron can be stripped away, leaving oxygen with no electrons and a charge of +8.

boxes.text: Why does each step need a higher temperature? Each step breaks a stronger link: the loose bonds between neighbouring molecules first, then the bonds inside molecules, then the grip of the nucleus on its electrons. Stronger links need more energy of motion to break.
Order from cold to hot: Melt, Evaporate, Dissociate, Ionize (M, E, D, I).

The temperature labels on slide 7 are placed loosely: they run from hundreds of K at the bottom to millions of K at the top. The textbook text says water becomes a plasma at 'several thousand degrees' but its Fig 5.10 puts a fully ionized plasma at millions of K, so do not memorize exact numbers. Practice test 2 Q19 explanation: ionizing needs thousands of K. Slide wording: dissociation = molecules into atoms; the textbook notes water first loses one H to leave OH, which then splits.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 5.3 (Molecular Dissociation and Ionization, Fig 5.10)

Ionization example (oxygen: O+, O2+, charge +8; hydrogen ionized once) is from Cosmic Perspective 5.3, Molecular Dissociation and Ionization (p.148). The ladder picture is the textbook Fig 5.10, which carries the same order as slide 7.

images.alt: A tall red arrow labelled increasing temperature, with pictures of the solid, liquid, gas, molecular dissociation, plasma and fully ionized plasma stages stacked from bottom to top.

sections.title: Energy levels and photon jumps
sections.slides: Matter deck (Ch5.3_PropertiesOfMatter.pdf) slides 8-9; Cosmic Perspective 5.3 Fig 5.12 and 5.4 Fig 5.15a

img.alt: Energy level diagram for hydrogen: level 1 at 0 eV, level 2 at 10.2 eV, level 3 at 12.1 eV, level 4 at 12.8 eV and the ionization level at 13.6 eV, with arrows between levels.

steps.title: Energy levels in hydrogen
bullets: Electrons in atoms can only have certain energies called **energy levels**, like rungs on a ladder.
The lowest level is the **ground state** (level 1, 0 eV). All higher levels are **excited states**: 10.2, 12.1 and 12.8 eV and so on, up to 13.6 eV where the electron escapes.
Each element has its own set of levels.

img.alt: The same hydrogen energy levels with labelled arrows: a 5 eV and an 11 eV photon are not accepted, exactly 10.2 eV lifts the electron to level 2, and a bigger jump frees it.

steps.title: Which jumps are allowed
bullets: An atom gains energy by absorbing a photon and loses energy by emitting one.
The photon energy must match the gap between two levels exactly. Level 1 to level 2 needs 10.2 eV.
If the energy does not match a gap, nothing happens. A 5 eV or an 11 eV photon is not absorbed by an atom in level 1.

img.alt: Hydrogen energy levels with downward arrows, each labelled with the wavelength of the photon it emits, such as 656.3 nm and 121.6 nm.

steps.title: Each jump has its own colour
bullets: When an electron falls, the photon carries away exactly the gap, so each jump gives one exact wavelength. Level 2 to level 1 gives 121.6 nm (ultraviolet). Level 3 to level 2 gives 656.3 nm (red).
A **bigger gap** means a more energetic photon and a **shorter wavelength**. The gap 10.2 eV is about 5 times the gap 1.9 eV, and 121.6 nm is about 5 times shorter than 656.3 nm.
Higher up, the gaps get smaller: 10.2, then 1.9, then 0.7 eV, so those photons have longer wavelengths (1875 nm for level 4 to level 3).

boxes.text: Why only certain energies? Electrons are restricted to discrete levels, and energy must be conserved. So a photon can only be absorbed if it supplies exactly the gap, and an emitted photon carries away exactly the gap.
Ladder, not ramp. You can stand on a rung but not between rungs, and an electron can sit on a level but not between levels.

Too much energy is refused too, not only too little: 11 eV is rejected because it falls between 10.2 and 12.1. The exception is a photon of 13.6 eV or more, which ionizes the atom; the extra energy becomes motion of the free electron (textbook). The gaps shrink higher up: 10.2, then 1.9, then 0.7 eV. The slide diagrams show hydrogen's levels without naming hydrogen; the textbook (Fig 5.12) confirms them.

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 5.3 (Energy Levels in Atoms, Fig 5.12)
Practice questions Q26 (12.1 eV hits level 1: jumps to level 3)

Third step (jump wavelengths, bigger gap = shorter wavelength) is from Cosmic Perspective Fig 5.15a; photon energy and wavelength are linked by E = hc/lambda (section 5.2). Check: 10.2/1.9 = 5.4 and 656.3/121.6 = 5.4.

sections.title: The Doppler effect
sections.slides: Doppler deck (Ch5.4_Doppler.pdf) slide 1; Cosmic Perspective 5.4 Fig 5.21c

img.alt: Two pictures of a train with circular waves spreading out: one still, one moving to the right, with longer waves behind it and shorter waves in front.

steps.title: Waves from a moving source
bullets: The **Doppler effect** is a shift in the wavelength (and frequency) of a wave whenever its source is moving relative to the observer.
Source moving **away**: the wavelength is **increased** (stretched).
Source moving **toward** you: the wavelength is **decreased** (squeezed).

img.alt: A light source in the middle: the person on the left sees redder light of longer wavelength, the person on the right sees bluer light of shorter wavelength.

steps.title: Light does the same
bullets: Light waves from a moving source are stretched or squeezed in the same way. A source moving **away** from you looks redder (longer wavelength).
A source moving **toward** you looks bluer (shorter wavelength).
For everyday speeds the shift is far too small for the eye to notice, so astronomers measure it in spectra.

boxes.text: Why does it happen? Each wave crest is let go from a new spot. A source coming toward you lets each crest go a bit closer to you than the last, so crests bunch up (shorter wavelength). A source moving away lets each crest go farther off, so they spread out (longer wavelength).
Train whistle: 'weeee' while it comes at you (high pitch, short waves), then 'oooh' as it leaves (low pitch, long waves).
Slide 1 labels the picture 'Increased wavelength' behind the train and 'Decreased wavelength' in front of it. For light, the shifts are usually too small to notice with the eye (textbook).

images.alt: Two pictures of a train with circular waves spreading out: one still, one moving to the right, with longer waves behind it and shorter waves in front.
A light source in the middle: the person on the left sees redder light of longer wavelength, the person on the right sees bluer light of shorter wavelength.

img.alt: Five black spectra with three coloured lines each: lines at rest positions, then shifted right a little and a lot for moving away, and shifted left a little and a lot for moving toward.

steps.title: Reading a shifted spectrum
bullets: A **spectral line** is a thin line at one exact wavelength. For a still object, each line sits at its normal 'rest' position.
Moving **away**: every line moves toward longer wavelengths, a **redshift**. Moving **toward** us: lines move to shorter wavelengths, a **blueshift**.
A bigger shift means a faster speed. A large redshift is moving away faster.

boxes.text: Why are spectral lines good speedometers? Each element makes lines at known wavelengths, measured in laboratory experiments. Compare where a line appears with where it should be, and the size of the gap tells you the speed.
Red = Receding (going away). Blue = Bearing down on us (coming closer).

Redshift and blueshift only describe the direction of the wavelength change; astronomers use the words even for ultraviolet or radio light. Textbook example: a line with rest wavelength 121.6 nm (ultraviolet) seen at 120.5 nm is a blueshift because the wavelength got shorter. On slide 2 the wavelength axis points right, so redshifted lines drift right.

images.alt: Five black spectra with three coloured lines each: lines at rest positions, then shifted right a little and a lot for moving away, and shifted left a little and a lot for moving toward.

sections.title: Only toward or away counts
sections.slides: Doppler deck (Ch5.4_Doppler.pdf) slide 3; Cosmic Perspective 5.4 Fig 5.23

img.alt: Earth with three stars: star 1 moving straight away, star 2 moving across the line of sight, and star 3 moving diagonally away with its speed split into a toward-away part and a sideways part.

steps.title: Three stars, same speed
bullets: The Doppler shift tells us only about the part of the motion directly **toward or away** from us.
Star 1 moves straight away, so its shift gives its full speed. Star 3 moves diagonally, so its shift gives only the 'away' part of its speed.
An object moving **perpendicular** to us (like star 2) has no Doppler shift at all.

boxes.text: Why does sideways motion not count? A Doppler shift comes from the distance to us changing, which squeezes or stretches the wave crests. Moving across our line of sight does not change the distance, so nothing is squeezed or stretched.
The Doppler shift is like a radar gun: it only reads the speed along the line between the object and you.

Zero shift does NOT mean the object is standing still; it may be moving purely sideways. The textbook adds that sideways speed has to be found by watching the position change in the sky over time. The 'distance does not change' wording is the standard reasoning, not from the slide (outside source).

images.alt: Earth with three stars: star 1 moving straight away, star 2 moving across the line of sight, and star 3 moving diagonally away with its speed split into a toward-away part and a sideways part.

sections.title: Spinning galaxies and stars
sections.slides: Doppler deck (Ch5.4_Doppler.pdf) slide 4; Cosmic Perspective 5.4 Fig 5.24

img.alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a blue wave on its left side, a red wave on its right side and an arrow showing how it spins.

steps.title: One side comes, one side goes
bullets: In an edge-on spinning galaxy, one side moves **toward** us (blueshift) and the other side moves **away** (redshift).
Measuring the Doppler shifts on both sides gives the galaxy's **rotation rate**.
The middle of the galaxy turns in place, so it shows no shift.

img.alt: Two stars, A rotating slowly and B rotating faster, each with blueshifted light from the approaching side and redshifted light from the receding side.

steps.title: A spinning star seen as a dot
bullets: Light from the part of a spinning star moving toward us is blueshifted, and light from the part moving away is redshifted. Light from the centre is not shifted.
Star B spins faster than star A, so its light is shifted farther to the blue and to the red.

img.alt: Graphs of intensity against wavelength: a narrow spectral line for the slowly rotating star and a broad spectral line for the faster rotating star.

steps.title: Faster spin means wider lines
bullets: We cannot see the two sides apart, so their light blends into one spectral line. The shifted light spreads the line over a range of wavelengths, so it looks **wider**.
A fast spinner gives a broad line and a slow spinner gives a narrow line. So line width measures the rotation rate.

boxes.text: Why is the centre not shifted? Spinning carries the middle around in place, so it moves neither toward nor away from us. Only the two edges have motion along our line of sight.
Think of a merry-go-round seen from the side: the child coming at you is blue, the child leaving you is red.

Rotation makes spectral lines wider, not thinner, and the blue and red sides stay fixed; they do not flip back and forth (practice test 2 Q24 explanation). The widening effect for a single dot is from the textbook (Fig 5.24), not slide 4. On slide 4 the left side is blue and the right side is red.

images.alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a blue wave on its left side, a red wave on its right side and an arrow showing how it spins.
Two stars, A rotating slowly and B rotating faster, each with blueshifted light from the approaching side and redshifted light from the receding side.
Graphs of intensity against wavelength: a narrow spectral line for the slowly rotating star and a broad spectral line for the faster rotating star.

sections.title: Doppler speed calculation
sections.slides: Doppler deck (Ch5.4_Doppler.pdf) pages 1-2 (idea); formula from Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.3

steps.title: The speed formula
bullets: For speeds well below the speed of light: **v / c = (seen - rest) / rest**, where 'rest' is the normal wavelength of a line and 'seen' is the wavelength you measure. Use c = 3 x 10^5 km/s.
A **positive** answer means redshift and moving **away**. A **negative** answer means blueshift and moving **toward** us.
The shift is a fraction of the rest wavelength, and that same fraction of the speed of light is the speed. A 0.1% shift means 0.1% of c = 300 km/s.

steps.title: Worked examples
bullets: A hydrogen line with rest wavelength 121.6 nm seen at 122.9 nm: (122.9 - 121.6) / 121.6 = 0.0107, so v = about +3,200 km/s, moving away.
Same line seen at 120.5 nm: (120.5 - 121.6) / 121.6 = -0.00905, so v = about -2,700 km/s, moving toward us.

steps.title: Going backwards: find the shift
bullets: You can also start from a known speed. The shift in wavelength is **rest wavelength x (v / c)**.
Example: a line with rest wavelength 600 nm from a star moving toward us at 150 km/s. v / c = 150 / 300,000 = 0.0005. Shift = 600 x 0.0005 = 0.3 nm.
Moving toward us shortens the wavelength, so the line is seen at 600 - 0.3 = 599.7 nm.

boxes.text: Why divide by the rest wavelength? What matters is how big the shift is compared with the original wavelength. A line shifted by 1% means the object moves at about 1% of the speed of light.
Say it as: 'seen minus rest, over rest, times c'. If seen is bigger than rest, the answer is positive and the object is going away.

The slides give no formula, only the idea that a bigger shift means a faster speed and the redshift or blueshift names. The formula, the c = 3 x 10^5 km/s value, the Vega example and the hydrogen 121.6 nm example are from the textbook (Mathematical Insight 5.3; end-of-chapter problems 49 and 61). The formula works only for speeds below a few percent of c. Keep the sign: negative means toward us.

sourceNotes: No slide gives the formula (slides 1-2 only say a bigger shift means a faster speed).
Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.3 and problem 61 (formula and numbers)
Backwards step: the formula rearranged (Mathematical Insight 5.3); the 600 nm and 150 km/s numbers are made up for practice (outside source).

sections.title: Three kinds of spectra
sections.slides: Doppler deck (Ch5.4_Doppler.pdf) slide 5; Cosmic Perspective 5.4 Figs 5.14-5.17

img.alt: Three set-ups with a prism: a hot light source gives a smooth rainbow, a warm gas cloud gives bright lines on black, and a hot source behind a cooler gas cloud gives dark lines on a rainbow, each with an intensity graph.

steps.title: Continuous, emission, absorption
bullets: **Continuous spectrum**: a smooth rainbow with no gaps. It comes from a hot, dense source such as a light bulb or the Sun's interior.
**Emission line spectrum**: bright lines at certain wavelengths on a dark background. It comes from a thin, warm gas seen with no bright source behind it.
**Absorption line spectrum**: dark lines on top of a rainbow. It comes from a bright continuous source seen through a cooler gas.

img.alt: Two hydrogen spectra with lines marked at 410.1, 434.0, 486.1 and 656.3 nm: bright lines on black on top, and dark lines on a rainbow below.

steps.title: Same lines, bright or dark
bullets: In a warm gas, collisions lift electrons to higher levels. They fall back and emit photons at exact wavelengths: bright **emission lines**.
A cooler gas in front of a bright source absorbs only photons that match its jumps. It re-emits them in random directions, so few reach us: dark **absorption lines**.
The top spectrum (emission) and bottom spectrum (absorption) of hydrogen show lines at the same four wavelengths: 410.1, 434.0, 486.1 and 656.3 nm. They are the same jumps in opposite directions.

img.alt: Emission line spectra of helium, sodium and neon as rows of coloured lines on black, each with a different pattern.

steps.title: Spectral fingerprints
bullets: Each atom and ion has its own set of energy levels, so it has a unique **spectral fingerprint**.
The helium, sodium and neon spectra show completely different line patterns.
So we can work out the **chemical composition** of a light-emitting object by reading its spectrum.

img.alt: A strip of ultraviolet spectrum with many bright blue lines on black, some labelled He, O and Ne, and a row of hydrogen lines underneath.

steps.title: Reading a real cloud
bullets: This spectrum of the Orion Nebula has many bright lines on a dark background, so the nebula is a thin, warm gas glowing on its own.
Lines are labelled He, O and Ne, with many more from hydrogen, so the cloud contains helium, oxygen, neon and hydrogen.
Different ions of one element make different lines, so the pattern also helps reveal how hot the gas is.

boxes.text: Why does a cool gas in front of a hot source leave dark lines? The atoms take out only the photons that match their energy gaps. Those photons are then sent off in all directions, so far fewer travel on toward us than before, and the rainbow shows dark gaps at those wavelengths.
Bright lines = the gas glowing on its own (emission). Dark lines = the gas standing in front of a light (absorption). On a graph, emission shows as spikes and absorption as dips.

Cool gas in front of a continuous source gives an ABSORPTION spectrum, not a continuous one and not an emission one (practice test 2 Q21). A thin warm gas with no bright source behind it gives EMISSION lines (practice questions Q27). The Sun's dark lines come from cooler, thinner outer gas absorbing light from the hotter interior (practice questions Q30). The slide only lists the three spectrum types; the reasons are from the textbook (Figs 5.14-5.15).

sourceNotes: Cosmic Perspective 5.4 (three basic types of spectra, Figs 5.14-5.17)
Practice test 2 Q21; practice questions Q27, Q30

Pictures are textbook Figs 5.14, 5.15b-c, 5.16 and 5.17 (slide 5 has no picture). The Orion Nebula reading and the ion-temperature remark are from the textbook (Fig 5.17 and the Chemical Fingerprints text).

sections.title: Thermal spectra and temperature
sections.slides: Doppler deck (Ch5.4_Doppler.pdf) slide 6; Cosmic Perspective 5.4 Figs 5.19-5.20 and Mathematical Insight 5.2

img.alt: Graph of intensity against wavelength with four smooth curves for a 15,000 K star, the Sun, a 3000 K star and a 310 K human; hotter curves are higher and peak at shorter wavelengths.

steps.title: Hotter means bluer peak
bullets: Practically all large objects (stars, planets, rocks, even people) give off a smooth **thermal spectrum**. Its shape depends only on temperature.
The peak of a hotter object sits at a **shorter wavelength**. The 3000 K star peaks in the infrared, the Sun (5800 K) in visible light and the 15,000 K star in the ultraviolet.
Each square metre of a hotter object emits more light at every wavelength. Notice that the human (310 K) curve peaks in the infrared.

img.alt: Four fireplace pokers in a fire, from a cool dark one to a glowing red one to a white-hot one, with notes on getting brighter and changing from red to white.

steps.title: A glowing poker
bullets: A cool poker gives off only infrared light that we cannot see. As it gets hotter it begins to glow, first red.
It gets brighter as it heats up (more light per square metre), and its colour changes from red to white (the peak moves to shorter wavelengths).
A person (310 K) glows mostly in the infrared, so we cannot see it, and a 3000 K star looks red-orange.

steps.title: The two formulas
bullets: **Stefan-Boltzmann law**: emitted power per square metre = sigma x T^4, where sigma = 5.7 x 10^-8 watt/(m^2 K^4) and T is in kelvin.
**Wien's law**: peak wavelength = 2,900,000 K nm / T (in nm). For the Sun, 2,900,000 / 5800 = 500 nm, which is green light.
Doubling the temperature makes each square metre emit 2^4 = 16 times more light and moves the peak to half the wavelength.

steps.title: Worked example: 10,000 K
bullets: Power per square metre: T^4 = (10,000)^4 = 10^16, so sigma x T^4 = 5.7 x 10^-8 x 10^16 = 5.7 x 10^8 watt/m^2, which is 570 million watts per square metre.
Peak wavelength: 2,900,000 / 10,000 = 290 nm, in the ultraviolet.
Used backwards, a spectrum that peaks at 290 nm means a surface temperature of about 10,000 K.

boxes.text: Why does the shape depend only on temperature? Inside a dense object, photons bounce around and share energy with the atoms until their energies match the atoms' average motion. That average motion is the temperature, whatever the object is made of.
Red-hot is cooler, white-hot is hotter. Cool stars look red, hot stars look blue-white.

A peak at a SHORTER wavelength means HOTTER, not cooler (practice test 2 Q23). The 'more light per square metre' law is per unit area: a very big 3000 K star can emit more total light than a small 15,000 K star (textbook). Slide 6 states only the peak rule; the examples, the per-area law and both formulas are from the textbook (Figs 5.19-5.20, Mathematical Insight 5.2). Practice questions Q28: temperature doubled means 2^4 = 16 times more light per square metre. Wien's law as given in practice test 2 Q23 explanation: peak = 2,900,000 / T.
Two laws, one idea: hotter means brighter (power goes as T to the 4th) and bluer (peak wavelength goes as 1 / T). Double the temperature: 16 times brighter, half the peak wavelength.

sourceNotes: Formulas and the 10,000 K worked example (5.7 x 10^8 watt/m^2 and 290 nm) are from Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.2. Sun at 5800 K gives 500 nm (matches the text).

cards.front: How to find an atom's charge
cards.back: Charge = number of protons minus number of electrons. A neutral atom has equal numbers, and losing electrons leaves a positive ion.

cards.front: What decides the phase of a substance?
cards.back: Both temperature and pressure. Temperature is the main driver, but squeezing a gas can turn it into a liquid.
cards.src: Matter deck slide 5; practice test 2 Q19

cards.back: A hot gas of ions and free electrons, made when atoms are ionized. Found in lightning and stars.
cards.short: Ionized gas of ions and electrons

cards.back: An exotic phase of matter reached near 0 Kelvin.
Breaking of rigid chemical bonds, changing a solid into a liquid.
cards.short: Rigid bonds break: solid to liquid

cards.back: Breaking of flexible chemical bonds, turning a liquid into a gas.
cards.short: Flexible bonds break: liquid to gas

cards.back: The breaking of molecules into atoms.
The stripping of electrons from atoms, which makes a plasma of ions.

cards.front: Order of phase changes as temperature rises
cards.back: Melting, evaporation, dissociation, ionization (solid, liquid, gas, atoms, plasma).
Electrons in atoms can only have certain, discrete energies, like rungs of a ladder. These levels are unique to each element.
The lowest energy level of an atom (level 1, 0 eV in hydrogen).
Any energy level above the ground state. In hydrogen: 10.2, 12.1, 12.8 eV and so on up to 13.6 eV.
cards.short: Any level above the ground state
cards.src: Matter deck slide 8; Cosmic Perspective Fig 5.12

cards.back: Level 1 = 0, level 2 = 10.2, level 3 = 12.1, level 4 = 12.8, ionization level = 13.6 eV.

cards.front: When can an atom absorb or emit a photon?
cards.back: Only when the photon energy exactly equals the gap between two energy levels. Otherwise no transition happens.
cards.short: Photon energy must match a level gap

cards.front: Energy needed to take hydrogen from level 1 to level 2
cards.back: 10.2 eV. A 5 eV or 11 eV photon will not be absorbed by an atom in level 1.
A shift in the wavelength or frequency of a wave whenever its source moves relative to the observer.
cards.short: Wave shift caused by source motion

cards.front: Source moving away: what happens to wavelength?
cards.back: The wavelength is increased (stretched). For light this is a redshift.

cards.front: Source moving toward you: what happens to wavelength?
cards.back: The wavelength is decreased (squeezed). For light this is a blueshift.

cards.front: What does a bigger Doppler shift mean?
cards.back: A faster speed. A large redshift means moving away faster; a large blueshift means moving toward us faster.

cards.front: What part of motion does the Doppler shift measure?
cards.back: Only the part directly toward or away from us.

cards.front: Object moving perpendicular to our line of sight
cards.back: It has no Doppler shift at all.
One side moves toward us (blueshift) and the other moves away (redshift). Comparing both sides gives the rotation rate.
cards.short: One side blue, other side red
cards.src: Doppler deck slide 4; practice test 2 Q24

cards.front: Rotating star seen as a single dot
cards.back: Its spectral lines look broader, and the faster it spins the broader they are.
cards.src: Cosmic Perspective Fig 5.24 (not on the slides)

cards.back: v / c = (seen wavelength - rest wavelength) / rest wavelength, with c = 3 x 10^5 km/s. Positive = moving away, negative = moving toward us.
cards.src: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.3 (formula not on slides)

cards.back: A smooth rainbow with no gaps, from a hot dense source such as a light bulb.
Bright lines at specific wavelengths on a dark background, from a thin warm gas seen without a bright source behind it.
Dark lines on a continuous rainbow, made when a bright source shines through a cooler gas.
cards.src: Doppler deck slide 5; practice test 2 Q21

cards.back: Each atom or ion has a unique set of lines, so spectra reveal the chemical composition of a light-emitting object.
cards.short: Unique line pattern of each element

cards.front: What does the shape of a thermal spectrum tell us?
cards.back: The object's temperature. A peak at shorter wavelengths means a hotter object.
Practically all large objects, such as stars, planets, rocks and people.

cards.front: Wien's law (peak wavelength of a thermal spectrum)
cards.back: Peak wavelength is about 2,900,000 K nm divided by the temperature T in kelvin. Hotter means a shorter peak wavelength.
cards.src: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.2; practice test 2 Q23 explained

cards.front: Stefan-Boltzmann law (light from each square metre)
cards.back: Emitted power per square metre = sigma x T^4, with sigma = 5.7 x 10^-8 watt/(m^2 K^4) and T in kelvin.
cards.short: Power per square metre = sigma T^4

cards.front: A star's temperature doubles. What happens to the light from each square metre, and to the peak wavelength?
cards.back: It becomes 2^4 = 16 times brighter per square metre, and the peak wavelength halves.
cards.short: Double T: 16 times brighter, half peak
cards.src: Practice questions Q28; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.2

cards.front: Vega's hydrogen line: rest 656.285 nm, seen 656.255 nm
cards.back: (656.255 - 656.285) / 656.285 = -4.57 x 10^-5. Times c gives -13.7 km/s: Vega moves toward us at 13.7 km/s.
cards.short: Vega moves toward us at 13.7 km/s

cards.back: O+ lost 1 electron (7 left, charge +1). O2+ lost 2 (6 left, charge +2). With all 8 electrons gone the charge is +8.

cards.front: How to find the wavelength shift from a known speed
cards.back: Shift = rest wavelength x (v / c). Moving away adds the shift (redshift); moving toward subtracts it (blueshift).
cards.short: Shift in nm = rest x v / c

quiz.q: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are ______.
quiz.why: Both have 6 protons, so both are carbon, but they have 6 and 8 neutrons. Same protons with different neutrons means isotopes.
quiz.source: Matter deck slide 4; practice questions Q25

quiz.q: An atom of doubly ionized calcium-44 has 20 protons, 24 neutrons and 18 electrons. What are its atomic number, atomic mass number and charge?
quiz.why: Atomic number = protons = 20. Mass number = protons + neutrons = 20 + 24 = 44. Charge = protons - electrons = 20 - 18 = +2.
quiz.source: Matter deck slides 3-4; practice test 2 Q18

quiz.q: A chloride ion, Cl-, has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. How many electrons does it have, and what is its atomic mass number?
quiz.why: Charge = protons - electrons, so -1 = 17 - electrons, which gives 18 electrons. The mass number counts only protons and neutrons: 17 + 18 = 35. Electrons never add to the mass number.
quiz.source: Matter deck slides 3-4 (Cl- ion); Cosmic Perspective 5.3 atomic terminology (same method as practice test 2 Q18)

quiz.q:
Oxygen has 8 protons. Which of the following statements are correct?
I. Singly ionized oxygen, O+, has 7 electrons.
II. A hydrogen atom can be ionized twice.
III. Oxygen with every electron stripped away has a charge of +8.
quiz.why: A neutral oxygen atom has 8 electrons, so O+ has 7. Hydrogen has only one electron, so it can be ionized just once. Stripping all 8 electrons from 8 protons leaves a charge of +8.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.3, Molecular Dissociation and Ionization (p.148)

quiz.q: What might happen to a gas if its pressure is increased while its temperature stays the same?
options: It could change phase into a liquid.
It could change phase into a plasma.
quiz.why: Phase depends on pressure as well as temperature. Squeezing pushes the molecules together so they can bond into a liquid. Ionization and plasma need very high temperature.
quiz.source: Matter deck slide 5; practice test 2 Q19

quiz.q: Earth's surface is far cooler than the boiling point of water, yet our air contains water vapor. What is the best explanation?
options: Water vapor in the air comes only from boiling water in volcanoes and hot springs.
The pressure at sea level is high enough to turn liquid water into a gas.
Sunlight ionizes the ocean water, and the ions then float up as vapor.
Ocean water molecules dissociate into hydrogen and oxygen atoms, which recombine as vapor.
Temperature is only the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so a few water molecules always have enough energy to break free of their neighbours.
quiz.why: Individual molecules can have far more or far less energy than the average. Even in cold water a few molecules always have enough energy to escape, so evaporation never stops completely.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.3 (Phase Changes in Water, p.147; Fig 5.11)

quiz.q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Squeezing a gas at constant temperature can never change its phase, because phase depends only on temperature.
Some water molecules in liquid water always have enough energy to escape as vapor, even well below the boiling point.
Calling the Sun a ball of hot plasma and calling it a ball of hot gas are both acceptable.
The rate at which water vapor molecules return to the ocean depends on the pressure that the water vapor exerts.
In molecular dissociation, collisions become violent enough to break the bonds that hold molecules together.
quiz.why: Phase depends on pressure as well as temperature, so squeezing a gas can turn it into a liquid. The other four statements match the descriptions of evaporation, plasma, vapor pressure and dissociation.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.3 pp.147-149 (Figs 5.10-5.11); Matter deck slide 5

quiz.q:
A sealed container of ice is heated to an extremely high temperature. Three things happen:
I. Electrons are stripped from atoms.
II. Bonds between neighbouring molecules break (melting, then evaporation).
III. Molecules split into separate atoms.
In which order do they happen as the temperature rises?
quiz.why: The weak bonds between molecules break first, then the stronger bonds inside molecules, and last the pull of each nucleus on its electrons. Each step needs more violent collisions than the one before.
quiz.source: Matter deck slide 7; Cosmic Perspective 5.3 (Fig 5.10)

quiz.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom is in level 1 (the ground state). A photon with exactly 12.1 eV of energy hits it. What happens?
options: The photon passes through without being absorbed.
quiz.why: Level 3 sits at 12.1 eV above the ground state, so the photon energy matches that gap exactly and the electron is lifted to level 3.
quiz.source: Matter deck slides 8-9; practice questions Q26

img.alt: Hydrogen energy level diagram: level 1 at 0 eV, level 2 at 10.2 eV, level 3 at 12.1 eV, level 4 at 12.8 eV, ionization level at 13.6 eV.

quiz.q: A hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a 14.6 eV photon. The ionization level is 13.6 eV. What happens?
options: The electron escapes and carries off the extra 1.0 eV as motion.
The photon is refused because it is too big.
The electron escapes with 14.6 eV of motion.
The electron escapes with 0 eV of motion.
quiz.why: 13.6 eV frees the electron, so the 14.6 - 13.6 = 1.0 eV left over becomes motion of the free electron.
quiz.source: Matter deck slide 8 (ionization level 13.6 eV); Cosmic Perspective 5.3

quiz.q: An electron in level 4 of a hydrogen atom (12.8 eV) falls to level 2 (10.2 eV) in two steps, first to level 3 (12.1 eV). What photon energies are emitted, and how does their total compare with a direct jump from level 4 to level 2?
options: 2.6 eV, then 1.9 eV; the total is 4.5 eV.
0.7 eV, then 1.9 eV; the total of 2.6 eV equals the direct jump.
0.7 eV, then 1.9 eV; the total is smaller than the direct jump because energy is lost as heat.
12.8 eV, then 12.1 eV; the total is 24.9 eV.
0.7 eV, then 10.2 eV; the total is 10.9 eV.
quiz.why: Each photon carries away the gap it crosses: 12.8 - 12.1 = 0.7 eV, then 12.1 - 10.2 = 1.9 eV. Energy is conserved, so the total, 2.6 eV, equals the direct gap 12.8 - 10.2.
quiz.source: Matter deck slides 8-9 (level values); Cosmic Perspective 5.3 Think about it (2.6 eV) and conservation of energy

img.alt: Hydrogen energy level diagram: level 1 at 0 eV, level 2 at 10.2 eV, level 3 at 12.1 eV, level 4 at 12.8 eV, ionization level at 13.6 eV.

quiz.q: In hydrogen, the jump from level 2 to level 1 gives a photon of wavelength 121.6 nm, and the jump from level 3 to level 2 gives a photon of wavelength 656.3 nm. With level 1 = 0, level 2 = 10.2 eV and level 3 = 12.1 eV, which statement is correct?
options: The 656.3 nm photon has about 5 times more energy, because longer wavelengths carry more energy.
Both photons have the same energy; only their wavelengths differ.
The 121.6 nm photon has only about 1.2 times more energy, because 12.1 / 10.2 is about 1.2.
The 121.6 nm photon has about 5 times more energy, because a bigger energy gap gives a shorter wavelength.
The 656.3 nm photon has about 5 times more energy, because it is visible light.
quiz.why: The 2-to-1 gap is 10.2 eV and the 3-to-2 gap is 12.1 - 10.2 = 1.9 eV, about 5.4 times smaller. A bigger gap gives a more energetic photon and a shorter wavelength; 121.6 nm is also about 5.4 times shorter than 656.3 nm.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.3 Fig 5.12 and 5.4 Fig 5.15a (wavelengths 121.6 and 656.3 nm); energy-wavelength link from 5.2

img.alt: Hydrogen energy levels with downward arrows labelled with the wavelengths of the photons they emit, such as 656.3 nm and 121.6 nm.

quiz.q: In hydrogen, the transition from level 3 down to level 2 gives an emission line at 656.3 nm. At what wavelength would hydrogen absorb light when its electron jumps from level 2 up to level 3?
options: It cannot absorb at this transition
quiz.why: Absorption and emission use the same energy gap in opposite directions, so the lines sit at the same wavelength.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 5 (unique fingerprint); Cosmic Perspective Fig 5.15

img.alt: Two hydrogen spectra with lines at 410.1, 434.0, 486.1 and 656.3 nm: bright lines on black above and dark lines on a rainbow below.

quiz.q: A continuous light source is placed behind a transparent container of cool atomic gas. A spectrometer in front of the container records the light. What kind of spectrum is obtained?
options: A continuous spectrum, because the light just passes through the gas.
An emission line spectrum, because the gas releases photons.
A continuous spectrum, because the source always dominates.
An absorption line spectrum, because the gas re-emits the absorbed photons in random directions, so few reach the spectrometer.
No spectrum, because the gas blocks all the light.
quiz.why: Cool atoms absorb only photons matching their energy gaps and send them out in random directions. Dark lines appear at those wavelengths on the rainbow.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 5; practice test 2 Q21

quiz.q: A thin, warm cloud of gas is observed with no bright light source behind it. What kind of spectrum do we see?
quiz.why: Collisions lift electrons to higher levels. When they fall back, they emit photons at exact wavelengths, giving bright lines on a dark background.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 5; practice questions Q27

quiz.q: An incandescent light bulb (filament at about 3000 K) shines through a glass prism. What do we see?
options: A rainbow practically identical to the one made by sunlight
A single yellowish colour at the wavelength given by the bulb
A rainbow with more red and orange than the rainbow from sunlight, because the filament is cooler than the Sun
A series of bright lines showing which chemicals are in the filament
Nothing, because a prism works only with sunlight
quiz.why: A hot, dense filament gives a continuous thermal spectrum: a full rainbow with no lines. At about 3000 K it is cooler than the Sun (5800 K), so its peak is at longer wavelengths and the rainbow leans toward red.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q22 (explained: continuous thermal spectrum, redder than sunlight); Cosmic Perspective 5.4 Fig 5.19

quiz.q: Why do we see dark absorption lines in the Sun's visible spectrum?
options: The Sun is moving away from Earth.
The Sun is too cool to emit those colours.
Cooler, thinner gas in the Sun's outer layer absorbs specific wavelengths from the hotter interior.
quiz.why: A hot, continuous light source seen through cooler gas gives an absorption line spectrum. For the Sun, the cooler gas is its outer layer.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 5; practice questions Q30; Cosmic Perspective 5.4

quiz.q: The picture shows part of the ultraviolet spectrum of the Orion Nebula, a glowing gas cloud. It has many bright lines on a dark background; some are labelled He, O and Ne and many others come from hydrogen. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The nebula is a hot, dense solid, because it produces bright lines.
The nebula is a thin, warm gas glowing on its own, and it contains hydrogen, helium, oxygen and neon.
The nebula sits in front of a bright continuous source, because it shows lines.
Only hydrogen is present, because hydrogen makes the most lines.
The lines show how fast the nebula is spinning, not what it is made of.
quiz.why: Bright lines on a dark background are an emission spectrum, which comes from a thin warm gas seen with no bright source behind it. Each element has its own pattern of lines, so the labelled lines show helium, oxygen and neon as well as hydrogen.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.4 Fig 5.17 and problem 48 (Orion Nebula, emission spectrum)

img.alt: Ultraviolet spectrum of the Orion Nebula with many bright lines on black, some labelled He, O and Ne, and a row of hydrogen lines.

quiz.q: Star A looks orange-red and star B looks yellow-white. Which statement is true?
options: Star A is hotter, since its light peaks at a longer wavelength.
Star A is hotter, since its light peaks at a shorter wavelength.
Star B is hotter, since its light peaks at a shorter wavelength.
Star B is cooler, since its light peaks at a shorter wavelength.
Both have the same temperature because both are stars.
quiz.why: A peak at a shorter wavelength means a hotter object. Yellow-white light peaks at a shorter wavelength than orange-red, so B is hotter.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 6; practice test 2 Q23

quiz.q: Two stars are the same size. Star X has a surface temperature of 10,000 K and star Y has a surface temperature of 5,000 K. How much more light does each square metre of star X emit?
quiz.why: The light from each square metre is proportional to T^4. Doubling the temperature gives 2^4 = 16 times more. A common slip is to forget the 4th power and say 2.
quiz.source: Practice questions Q28; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.2 (Stefan-Boltzmann law)

quiz.q: A 10,000 K object emits thermal radiation. Use emitted power per square metre = sigma x T^4 with sigma = 5.7 x 10^-8 W/(m^2 K^4), and peak wavelength = 2,900,000 K nm / T. What are the power per square metre and the peak wavelength?
quiz.why: T^4 = (10,000)^4 = 10^16, so 5.7 x 10^-8 x 10^16 = 5.7 x 10^8 W/m^2. Peak wavelength = 2,900,000 / 10,000 = 290 nm. Using T instead of T^4 would give only 5.7 x 10^-4.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.2 (worked example)

quiz.q: Star P has a surface temperature of 3000 K and a radius 100 times the radius of star Q, whose surface temperature is 15,000 K. Light per square metre goes as T^4 and surface area goes as radius squared. How does the total light output of P compare with Q?
options: P emits 16 times more total light than Q.
Q emits 625 times more total light, because it is hotter.
P emits 100 times more total light, because it is 100 times bigger.
Q emits 16 times more total light than P.
P emits 10,000 times more total light, because its area is 10,000 times bigger.
quiz.why: Per square metre, Q emits (15,000 / 3000)^4 = 5^4 = 625 times more than P. But P has 100^2 = 10,000 times more surface area. Net: 10,000 / 625 = 16 times more total light from the big, cool star.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.4 (Fig 5.19 text: a very large 3000 K star can emit more total light than a small 15,000 K star; Math Insight 5.2 surface area). The 100x radius is made up for practice (outside source).

quiz.q: A hydrogen line with a rest wavelength of 656.3 nm appears at 660.0 nm in a star's spectrum. What can we conclude?
options: The star is moving toward us.
The star is hotter than the Sun.
The star is cooler than the Sun.
The star is not moving relative to us.
The star is moving away from us.
quiz.why: 660.0 nm is longer than the rest wavelength, a redshift, so the star is moving away from us. Nothing here tells us its temperature.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slides 1-2; practice questions Q29

quiz.q: One visible line of hydrogen has a rest wavelength of 656.285 nm but appears at 656.255 nm in the spectrum of the star Vega. Use v = c x (seen - rest) / rest with c = 3 x 10^5 km/s. How is Vega moving?
quiz.why: (656.255 - 656.285) / 656.285 = -4.57 x 10^-5. Multiply by c: -4.57 x 10^-5 x 3 x 10^5 km/s = -13.7 km/s. The negative sign means a blueshift, so Vega moves toward us.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.3 (worked example, Vega)

quiz.q: The hydrogen line with rest wavelength 121.6 nm appears at 122.9 nm in a star's spectrum. Use v = c x (seen - rest) / rest with c = 3 x 10^5 km/s. What are the star's speed and direction?
quiz.why: (122.9 - 121.6) / 121.6 = 1.3 / 121.6 = 0.0107. Times 3 x 10^5 km/s gives about 3,200 km/s. A positive result means the wavelength grew, a redshift, so the star moves away.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective problem 61 part d (with Mathematical Insight 5.3)

quiz.q: A star moves toward us at 150 km/s. A spectral line that normally has a wavelength of 600 nm is observed at which wavelength? (Use c = 3 x 10^5 km/s.)
quiz.why: v / c = 150 / 300,000 = 0.0005, so the shift is 600 nm x 0.0005 = 0.3 nm. Moving toward us shortens the wavelength (blueshift), so the line appears at 600 - 0.3 = 599.7 nm.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 5.3 (formula rearranged); numbers made up (outside source)

quiz.q: The hydrogen line with rest wavelength 121.6 nm is seen at 120.5 nm in star A, 121.2 nm in star B, 121.9 nm in star C and 122.9 nm in star D. Without calculating, which statement is correct?
options: A and B move away from us, C and D move toward us, and D is fastest.
A and B move toward us, C and D move away, and A is the fastest of all four.
A and B move toward us, C and D move away, and D is the fastest of all four.
All four stars move away from us, and D is fastest.
A and B move toward us, C and D move away, and B is the fastest of all four.
quiz.why: A and B are shorter than 121.6 nm (blueshift, toward). C and D are longer (redshift, away). The biggest shift is D at +1.3 nm, bigger than A at -1.1 nm, so D is fastest.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 2; Cosmic Perspective problem 49

quiz.q:
Three stars move at the same speed. Star 1 moves directly away from us, star 2 moves across our line of sight, and star 3 moves diagonally away. Which statements are correct?
I. Star 1's Doppler shift gives its full speed.
II. Star 2 shows no Doppler shift.
III. Star 3's Doppler shift gives its full speed.
quiz.why: A Doppler shift shows only the toward-or-away part of the motion. That is the full speed for star 1, none of it for star 2, and just part of it for star 3.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 3; Cosmic Perspective Fig 5.23

img.alt: Earth with three stars: star 1 moving directly away, star 2 moving across the line of sight, star 3 moving diagonally away.

quiz.q: What spectral feature would we notice in a rotating galaxy viewed edge-on?
options: All of the spectral lines are blueshifted.
All of the spectral lines are redshifted.
Lines on one side are blueshifted and on the other side are redshifted.
The shifts flip back and forth between blue and red as the galaxy rotates.
quiz.why: One side of the spinning galaxy moves toward us (blueshift) and the other moves away (redshift). The rotation is steady, so the sides do not swap.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 4; practice test 2 Q24

img.alt: An edge-on spinning galaxy with a blue wave on the left and a red wave on the right.

quiz.q: A star spins quickly and appears to us as a single point of light. Compared with a slowly spinning star, how do its spectral lines look?
quiz.why: Light from the side moving toward us is blueshifted and from the side moving away is redshifted. Blended together, each line is spread over a wider range of wavelengths, more so for faster spin.
quiz.source: Doppler deck slide 4; Cosmic Perspective 5.4 (Fig 5.24) | rotation broadening is in textbook Fig 5.24 only

img.alt: Two spinning stars, A slowly and B faster, with blueshifted light from the approaching side and redshifted light from the receding side.

order.title: Heating water
order.prompt: Water is heated from very cold to extremely hot. Put the states in order as the temperature rises.
order.why: Weak bonds between molecules break first (melting, then evaporation), then the bonds inside molecules (dissociation), and last the electrons are stripped from atoms (ionization), which makes a plasma. Each step needs more violent collisions.

order.title: Hydrogen photons
order.prompt: In hydrogen, level 1 = 0 eV, level 2 = 10.2 eV, level 3 = 12.1 eV and level 4 = 12.8 eV. Each downward jump emits a photon equal to the gap. Order the jumps by photon energy.
order.why: The gaps are: level 4 to 3 = 0.7 eV, level 3 to 2 = 1.9 eV, level 4 to 2 = 2.6 eV, level 2 to 1 = 10.2 eV and level 3 to 1 = 12.1 eV. A bigger gap gives a more energetic photon with a shorter wavelength.

order.title: Doppler shifts
order.prompt: The hydrogen line with rest wavelength 121.6 nm is seen at these wavelengths in four stars. Order the stars by radial velocity, from moving toward us fastest to moving away fastest.
order.why: Shorter than 121.6 nm is a blueshift (toward us) and longer is a redshift (away). The size of the shift gives the speed: A is -1.1 nm (about 2,700 km/s toward), B is -0.4 nm (about 990 km/s toward), C is +0.3 nm (about 740 km/s away) and D is +1.3 nm (about 3,200 km/s away).

layers.name: Star A: line seen at 120.5 nm
Star B: line seen at 121.2 nm
Star C: line seen at 121.9 nm
Star D: line seen at 122.9 nm

order.title: Thermal peaks
order.prompt: Objects give off thermal spectra. Order them by the wavelength where their spectrum peaks.
order.why: Peak wavelength = 2,900,000 / T (in nm). A person (310 K) peaks near 9,400 nm, a 3000 K star near 970 nm, the Sun (5800 K) near 500 nm, a 10,000 K object near 290 nm and a 15,000 K star near 190 nm. Hotter means a shorter peak.

sort.title: Which kind of spectrum?
sort.prompt: Decide which spectrum each situation gives.
sort.why: Hot dense objects give a smooth continuous rainbow. A thin warm gas seen alone gives bright emission lines. A cooler gas in front of a bright source takes out its own wavelengths and leaves dark absorption lines.

A red-hot fireplace poker
The smooth glow of a hot, dense star interior

Hydrogen electrons falling from level 3 to level 2 and releasing 656.3 nm light
Bulb light shining through a cooler gas cloud
The Sun's rainbow with many dark lines

A hot star seen through a cooler cloud of gas in front of it

sort.title: Isotope, ion or new element?
sort.prompt: Decide what changes between the two atoms.
sort.why: Protons name the element. Different neutrons make an isotope. Different electrons make an ion.

He and He2+
Cl and Cl-

A hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron
An atom with 6 protons and an atom with 8 protons
A nucleus with 1 proton and a nucleus with 2 protons

sort.title: Redshift, blueshift or none?
sort.prompt: What Doppler shift does each situation give?
sort.why: A longer wavelength than the rest wavelength is a redshift (moving away). A shorter wavelength is a blueshift (moving toward us). Motion across our line of sight, or no motion along it, gives no shift.
